name: Augustine of Hippo
info: Augustine of Hippo (354–430) was a Christian theologian and philosopher from Thagaste in Roman Numidia and Bishop of Hippo Regius, remembered for the Confessions, The City of God and his teaching on grace and original sin.

facts.born: 13 November 354 at Thagaste, in the Roman province of Numidia (now Souk Ahras, Algeria); son of Patricius, a pagan who converted on his deathbed, and Monica, a devout Christian
facts.died: 28 August 430 at Hippo Regius (now Annaba, Algeria), during his final illness while the Vandals besieged the city
facts.role: Teacher of rhetoric at Thagaste, Carthage, Rome and Milan (373–386); priest at Hippo Regius (from 391); coadjutor bishop (395) and then Bishop of Hippo; one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers; a saint in the Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican traditions
facts.known: the Confessions, often called the first Western autobiography; The City of God; On the Trinity; his teaching on grace, original sin and predestination; his arguments against the Donatists; just war theory; his conversion in 386

t: Born in Thagaste to a pagan father and a Christian mother, Augustine became a teacher of rhetoric, spent years among the Manichaeans and was baptised by Ambrose at Milan in 387.
As priest and then bishop of Hippo from 391 and 395, he wrote the Confessions and The City of God, and argued against the Manichaeans, the Donatists and the Pelagians.
He supported the state's use of coercion against the Donatists, a position his modern defenders and detractors have found troubling, and he died in 430 while the Vandals besieged Hippo.
dyk: Augustine never mastered Greek: his first Greek teacher beat his students, and Augustine rebelled and refused to study. By the time he realised he needed it, it was too late, though he became a master of Latin.
ev: Born at Thagaste in Numidia, to a pagan father and a Christian mother
Takes up the post of professor of rhetoric at Milan, at thirty years old
Converts to Christianity after hearing a child's voice say "take up and read"
Baptised in Milan by Ambrose on Easter Vigil, together with his son Adeodatus
Ordained a priest at Hippo Regius
Made coadjutor Bishop of Hippo, and soon full bishop
Begins writing the Confessions, completed in 398
Dies on 28 August as the Vandals besiege Hippo

sections.early:
Augustine was born on 13 November 354 in the municipium of Thagaste, now Souk Ahras in Algeria, in the Roman province of Numidia. His mother Monica was a devout Christian; his father Patricius was a pagan who converted to Christianity on his deathbed. He had a brother, Navigius, and a sister whose name is lost. Scholars generally agree that the family were Berbers, heavily Romanised and speaking only Latin at home, and in his writings Augustine mentions in passing his identity as a Roman African.

At eleven he was sent to school at Madaurus, where he became familiar with Latin literature and with pagan beliefs and practices. In the Confessions he tells how he and some friends stole pears from a neighbour's garden, though he was neither hungry nor poor, and how he later brooded over the theft. At seventeen he went to Carthage to study rhetoric, through the generosity of his fellow citizen Romanianus, since the cost was beyond his family's means.

At Carthage he read Cicero's dialogue Hortensius, now lost, which he said kindled in him the love of wisdom. Raised a Christian, he became a Manichaean, much to his mother's chagrin. He began a relationship with a young woman that lasted more than fifteen years and produced a son, Adeodatus, born in 372. He never mastered Greek.
sections.rise:
Augustine taught grammar at Thagaste in 373–374, then ran a school of rhetoric at Carthage for nine years. Disturbed by unruly students, he moved to Rome in 383, hoping for better ones, but was disappointed: many students attended all term and then did not pay. Manichaean friends introduced him to Symmachus, the prefect of the City of Rome, who had been asked to find a rhetoric professor for the imperial court at Milan. Augustine won the post and took it up in late 384, at thirty, the most visible academic position in the Latin world.

He had been a Manichaean auditor, the lowest rank, and a disappointing meeting with the Manichaean bishop Faustus of Mileve had begun his doubts. At Milan his mother's piety, his own reading of the Neoplatonists and his friend Simplicianus drew him towards Christianity, and he came to know Ambrose, whom he first approached for his reputation as an orator.

Monica arranged a respectable marriage for him. Augustine had to send away his concubine and grieved for her; he recalled praying "Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet." In late August 386, at thirty-one, after hearing of Ponticianus's reading of the life of Anthony of the Desert, he heard a child's voice say "take up and read" and opened Paul's letters at Romans 13:13–14. Ambrose baptised him and Adeodatus in Milan on the Easter Vigil, 24–25 April 387.
sections.deeds:
In 388 Augustine and Adeodatus returned to Africa. Monica died at Ostia as they prepared to embark, and Adeodatus died soon after. Augustine sold his inheritance and gave the money to the poor, keeping only the family house, which he made a monastic foundation for himself and friends. In 391 he was ordained a priest at Hippo Regius, now Annaba, and in 395 he became coadjutor Bishop of Hippo and soon full bishop. He turned away from his profession as a teacher of rhetoric to preaching; more than 350 preserved sermons are believed authentic, and his sermons were taken down by stenographers.

He wrote the Confessions in 397–398. The City of God, in twenty-two books, was written to console fellow Christians after the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410. His other works include On the Trinity, On Christian Doctrine and On Free Choice of the Will, and in his last years the Retractationes, a review of his earlier writings. The list of his works runs to more than one hundred titles.

Against the Pelagians he taught that the sin of Adam and Eve wounded the human will and that unmerited grace was necessary for salvation. Against the Donatists he held that the validity of a sacrament does not depend on the holiness of the priest who performs it. In The City of God he coined the phrase "just war", arguing that war must be defensive and authorised by a legitimate authority.
sections.opponents:
In North Africa the Donatists, who refused to readmit clergy who had handed over sacred books under the Great Persecution, and the Catholics had stood side by side for decades, often with two bishops in one city. Donatists and Circumcellions carried out street violence, and in Letter 28, around 416, Augustine described Donatists cutting out the tongue and cutting off the hands of Bishop Rogatus, who had converted to Catholicism. Augustine first held that conversion must be voluntary and appealed in words, then supported the state's use of coercion. In Letter 93, written in 408, he said he changed his mind because of "the ineffectiveness of dialogue and the proven efficacy of laws."

He recommended fines, imprisonment, banishment and moderate floggings, and opposed maiming and the execution of heretics, though Roman authorities mostly ignored these limits. Herbert Deane found a fundamental inconsistency between this position and Augustine's political thought; Peter Brown called it more an attitude than a doctrine; Frederick Russell argued that it answered a unique historical situation and that later writers applied it far beyond it. Its critics have called him the prince and patriarch of persecutors.

The Pelagians denied that original sin wounded the human will. Augustine held that the sin of Adam is inherited by all and was the first to add the concept of inherited guilt. Patristics scholar Ken Wilson argues that he abandoned the free choice earlier Christians taught; the Catholic Church holds that his teaching is consistent with free will.
sections.last:
Shortly before Augustine's death the Vandals, a Germanic tribe that had converted to Arianism, invaded Roman Africa. They besieged Hippo in the spring of 430, as Augustine entered his final illness. According to his friend and biographer Possidius, bishop of Calama, one of the few miracles attributed to Augustine, the healing of an ill man, took place during the siege.

He spent his final days in prayer and repentance, and asked that the penitential Psalms be hung on his walls so that he could read them; Possidius says he wept freely and constantly. He directed that the library of the church in Hippo be carefully preserved. He died on 28 August 430. The Vandals lifted the siege soon after, but returned and burned the city, destroying all but Augustine's cathedral and library.

Augustine was canonised by popular acclaim and recognised as a Doctor of the Church by Pope Boniface VIII in 1298. His feast day is 28 August, also kept as a lesser festival in the Church of England. According to Bede's True Martyrology his body was taken to Cagliari in Sardinia by Catholic bishops expelled from North Africa, and around 720 it was moved to Pavia. In 1695 workmen at San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro found a box of bones, which the Bishop of Pavia declared to be Augustine's. In 1842 part of his right arm was returned to Annaba.
sections.legacy:
Augustine is a saint in the Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Lutheran churches and the Anglican Communion, and with Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory the Great is one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers. He was the most cited author in the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas. Many Protestants, especially Calvinists and Lutherans, consider him one of the theological fathers of the Reformation because of his teaching on grace, though the Catholic Church disputes this reading. In Eastern Orthodoxy he is venerated, while some of his teachings, among them the filioque, are more disputed.

The historian Diarmaid MacCulloch wrote that his impact on Western Christian thought "can hardly be overstated". His account of time in the Confessions drew Edmund Husserl's praise, and Hannah Arendt wrote her first dissertation on his concept of love; Ludwig Wittgenstein opened Philosophical Investigations with a passage from the Confessions. According to Leo Ruickbie, his arguments against magic later became central to the denunciation of witchcraft.

His views on sexuality and on slavery remain debated. He wrote that slavery was a result of sin and led clergy under him to free their slaves, but he also held it to be penal and urged slaves to serve in faithful love. He taught that Jews should not be slain or forcibly converted, because their scriptures bear witness to Christianity, a view that became Church policy; the saying that they should "survive but not thrive" is not found in his writings.

summary: Augustine of Hippo (354–430), born at Thagaste in Numidia, taught rhetoric, passed through Manichaeism and was baptised at Milan in 387. As Bishop of Hippo he wrote the Confessions and The City of God and shaped Western teaching on grace and original sin.
references: G. Bonner, St. Augustine of Hippo. Life and Controversies (The Canterbury Press, 1986)
Peter Brown, Augustine of Hippo: A Biography (University of California Press, 2000)
Henry Chadwick, Augustine of Hippo: A Life (Oxford University Press, 2010)
notes: Baptism: the lead says 'baptism in 386 by Saint Ambrose', but the Conversion section gives Easter Vigil, 24–25 April 387 (conversion in late August 386); the 387 date is used.
Manichaean years: the article says 'ten years' in one place and 'about nine years' in another; no number is given in the text.
Sermons: 'more than 350 preserved sermons are believed to be authentic' versus 'around 500 accessible today' and 6,000 to 10,000 preached; only the first figure is used.
Fiancée: described as a 'teenage heiress' and as 'eleven-year-old'; her age is left out.
Monica is said to follow Augustine to Milan; the Ambrose 'spiritual son' sentence was left out as a stray claim.
Letter 28 (c. 416) is dated by the article only as 'around 416' although Augustine's lifetime ordering places it after Letter 93 (408); both given as the article has them.
